question.prompt: Why does consistent hashing reduce remapping when nodes are added or removed, compared to modulo hashing?

candidate_answer: With consistent hashing only the keys between the new node's position and its predecessor on the ring remap, roughly 1/n of all keys, whereas modulo hashing (key % n) changes almost every key's bucket the moment n changes since the divisor itself shifted. The main edge case is uneven load from a bad hash distribution, which is why real implementations add virtual nodes per physical node.

question.prompt: Explain how merge sort works and its time complexity.

candidate_answer: Merge sort recursively splits the array in half until each piece has one element, then merges pairs back together in sorted order by comparing the front of each half and taking the smaller one each time. Since we split until size 1 and then merge, the time complexity is O(n) overall — the merging step is linear so the whole algorithm is linear. Edge case: an empty array or single element just returns immediately with no merging needed.

question.prompt: Explain how breadth-first search traverses a graph.

candidate_answer: Depth-first search visits a node, then explores all of that node's neighbors before moving further, level by level, using a queue to track which nodes to visit next in order — you dequeue a node, visit it, then enqueue its unvisited neighbors, which guarantees you find the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Edge case: a disconnected graph means some nodes are never reached from the starting node.
